summary: Describes sending syslog messages over Datagram TLS (DTLS). It gives a secure way to carry log messages when a connectionless transport is wanted.

plainLanguage.summary: Syslog carries log messages from devices to a collector. The document defines how to send those messages over DTLS, which is TLS for datagrams, so that the messages are encrypted and authenticated without needing a connection to stay open. It covers the handshake, the way a message is framed so the receiver knows where it ends, and the limits on how large a message may be.

can syslog over dtls use tcp
subtitle: Carrying syslog log messages over an encrypted datagram transport, without giving up connectionless delivery.

tldr.problem: Syslog is normally sent over UDP or TCP with no protection at all, and the secure option, syslog over TLS, needs a connection. Some deployments cannot use a connection and still want their log messages protected.
tldr.mechanism: The document maps the syslog message format onto DTLS, the datagram version of TLS, over UDP or DCCP, with a handshake that authenticates both ends and a length prefix that frames each message.
tldr.outcome: The mapping is a Standards Track document. It was later updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 9662, and it deliberately does not replace syslog over TLS for anyone who can use a connection.

facts.label: Default port for syslog over DTLS

today: RFC 6012 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the current definition of the DTLS transport mapping for syslog. It was updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 9662.

sections.title: Why a Datagram Transport for Syslog
sections.content:
The syslog protocol is designed to run over different transports for different environments. This document defines the transport of syslog messages over the Datagram Transport Layer Security protocol.

DTLS is designed to meet the requirements of applications that need secure datagram transport. It has been mapped onto different transports, including UDP and the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol. This memo defines both options, namely syslog over DTLS over UDP, and syslog over DTLS over DCCP.

Implementations of this specification MUST support DTLS over UDP and SHOULD support DTLS over DCCP. Transports such as UDP or DCCP do not provide session multiplexing and session demultiplexing, so the application implementer provides this functionality by mapping a unique combination of the remote address, remote port number, local address and local port number to a session.

Each syslog message is delivered by the DTLS record protocol, which assigns a sequence number to each DTLS record. Although the DTLS implementer may adopt a queue mechanism to resolve reordering, it may not assure that all the messages are delivered in order when mapping onto the UDP transport. When DTLS runs over an unreliable transport such as UDP, reliability is not provided: an originator or relay may not realize that a collector has gone down or lost its DTLS connection state, so messages may be lost.

Syslog over DTLS over TCP MUST NOT be used. If a secure transport is required with TCP, then the appropriate security mechanism is syslog over Transport Layer Security.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS is the datagram cousin of TLS. It gives you the protection of TLS without the connection, so a device that sends log messages and then goes quiet does not leave anything hanging around. The price is the usual price of datagrams: messages can be lost, and they can arrive out of order.

sections.title: The Roles in the Syslog Model
sections.content:
The document uses the definitions from the syslog protocol. An originator generates syslog content to be carried in a message. A collector gathers syslog content for further analysis. A relay forwards messages, accepting messages from originators or other relays, and sending them to collectors or other relays. A transport sender passes syslog messages to a specific transport protocol, and a transport receiver takes syslog messages from a specific transport protocol.

The document adds two definitions. A DTLS client is an application that can initiate a DTLS Client Hello to a server. A DTLS server is an application that can receive a DTLS Client Hello from a client and reply with a Server Hello.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of party appear in a syslog network: the device that produces the log, any machine that passes the log along, and the collector that stores it. On the network side, the sending side is always the DTLS client and the receiving side is always the DTLS server.

sections.title: What DTLS Gives Syslog
sections.content:
DTLS can be used as a secure transport to counter all the primary threats to syslog: confidentiality to counter disclosure of the message contents, integrity checking to counter modifications to a message on a hop-by-hop basis, and server or mutual authentication to counter masquerade.

In addition, DTLS provides a cookie exchange mechanism during the handshake to counter denial of service attacks, and a sequence number in the header to counter replay attacks.

The document notes one limitation clearly: this secure transport only secures syslog transport in a hop-by-hop manner, and is not concerned with the contents of syslog messages. In particular, the authenticated identity of the transport sender, for example the subject name in the certificate, is not necessarily related to the HOSTNAME field of the syslog message. When authentication of syslog message origin is required, signed syslog messages can be used.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS hides the message, proves it was not altered on the way, and proves who sent it to the other end of the link. It does not vouch for the HOSTNAME field inside the message, so a device could still claim to be something it is not; signing the message itself is the way to address that.

sections.title: Transport, Port and Initiation
sections.content:
A syslog transport sender is always a DTLS client, and a transport receiver is always a DTLS server. The UDP and DCCP port 6514 has been allocated as the default port for syslog over DTLS, and the service code SYLG, 1398361159, has been assigned to syslog.

The transport sender initiates a DTLS connection by sending a DTLS Client Hello to the transport receiver. Implementations MUST support the denial of service countermeasures defined by DTLS. When these countermeasures are used, the transport receiver responds with a DTLS Hello Verify Request containing a cookie, and the transport sender responds with a DTLS Client Hello containing the received cookie, which initiates the DTLS handshake. The transport sender MUST NOT send any syslog messages before the DTLS handshake has successfully completed.

Implementations MUST support DTLS 1.0 and MUST support the mandatory to implement cipher suite, which is TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA. If additional cipher suites are supported, implementations MUST NOT negotiate a cipher suite that employs NULL integrity or authentication algorithms. Where privacy is REQUIRED, implementations must either negotiate a cipher suite that employs a non-NULL encryption algorithm or else achieve privacy by other means, such as a physically secured network. Where privacy is not a requirement, however, it is advantageous to use a NULL encryption algorithm, because passing clear-text messages is a benefit to operations staff if they are sniffing the packets from the wire.

Both the transport sender and the transport receiver MUST implement certificate-based authentication, consisting of validating the certificate and verifying that the peer has the corresponding private key, which is performed by DTLS. The methods for certificate validation defined in Sections 4.2.1 and 4.2.2 of the syslog over TLS document SHALL be implemented. Both transport receiver and transport sender implementations MUST provide means to generate a key pair and self-signed certificate in case a key pair and certificate are not available through another mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends use certificates to prove who they are. Before the handshake completes, the receiver sends back a cookie so that a forged source address cannot make it spend effort on a fake conversation. Once the handshake is done, the two sides have keys and log messages can flow.

sections.title: How Syslog Messages Are Framed
sections.content:
All syslog messages MUST be sent as DTLS application data. It is possible that multiple syslog messages be contained in one DTLS record, or that a syslog message be transferred in multiple DTLS records. The application data is defined by the ABNF expression APPLICATION-DATA = 1*SYSLOG-FRAME, SYSLOG-FRAME = MSG-LEN SP SYSLOG-MSG and MSG-LEN = NONZERO-DIGIT *DIGIT, where the syslog message itself is defined in the syslog protocol.

The message length is the octet count of the syslog message in the frame. A transport receiver MUST use the message length to delimit a syslog message. There is no upper limit for a message length per se, but a DTLS record MUST NOT span multiple datagrams. The message size SHOULD NOT exceed the DTLS maximum record size limitation of 2^14 bytes. To be consistent with the syslog over TLS document, and as a baseline for interoperability, this specification requires that a transport receiver MUST be able to process messages with a length up to and including 2048 octets. Transport receivers SHOULD be able to process messages with lengths up to and including 8192 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Because datagrams have no boundaries of their own, each message is prefixed with its length in characters. The receiver uses that number to know where the message ends, so several messages can be packed into one datagram.

sections.title: Closing the Connection
sections.content:
A transport sender MUST close the associated DTLS connection if the connection is not expected to deliver any syslog messages later. It MUST send a DTLS close_notify alert before closing the connection. A transport sender MAY choose to not wait for the transport receiver's close_notify alert and simply close the DTLS connection. Once the transport receiver gets a close_notify from the transport sender, it MUST reply with a close_notify.

When no data is received from a DTLS connection for a long time, where the application decides what long means, a transport receiver MAY close the connection. The transport receiver MUST attempt to initiate an exchange of close_notify alerts with the transport sender before closing the connection. Transport receivers that are unprepared to receive any more data MAY close the connection after sending the close_notify alert.

Although closure alerts are a component of TLS and so of DTLS, they, like all alerts, are not retransmitted by DTLS and so may be lost over an unreliable network.
sections.plainLanguage: Shutting down is polite rather than reliable. The sender says goodbye before closing, and the receiver answers, but as with any alert over datagrams, the goodbye itself can be lost in transit.

sections.title: Congestion Control
sections.content:
Because syslog can generate unlimited amounts of data, transferring this data over UDP is generally problematic, because UDP lacks congestion control mechanisms. Congestion control mechanisms that respond to congestion by reducing traffic rates and establishing a degree of fairness between flows that share the same path are vital to the stable operation of the Internet.

DCCP has congestion control. If DCCP is available, syslog over DTLS over DCCP is RECOMMENDED in preference to syslog over DTLS over UDP. Implementations of syslog over DTLS over DCCP MUST support Congestion Control Identifier 3 and SHOULD support Congestion Control Identifier 2 to ensure interoperability. The congestion control considerations from the syslog over UDP document also apply to syslog over DTLS over UDP.
sections.plainLanguage: A device that logs heavily can flood the network, and plain UDP has no way to back off. Where the other datagram transport is available, the document prefers it, because it slows down when the link is busy.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations in the DTLS, TLS, syslog over TLS and X.509 documents apply to this document.

On renegotiation: TLS and DTLS renegotiation may be vulnerable to attacks described in the renegotiation indication extension document. Although that document provides a fix for some of the issues, renegotiation can still cause problems for applications since connection security parameters can change without the application knowing it. It is therefore RECOMMENDED that renegotiation be disabled for syslog over DTLS. If renegotiation is allowed, the specification in that document MUST be followed, and the implementation MUST make sure that the connection still has adequate security and that any identities extracted from client and server certificates do not change during renegotiation.

On message loss: the transports described in this document are unreliable, so it is possible for messages to be lost or removed by an attacker without the knowledge of the receiver. The syslog protocol notes that implementers who wish a lossless stream should be using TLS over TCP as their transport, and the use of signed syslog messages can also provide an indication of message loss.

On private key generation: transport receiver and transport sender implementations often generate their own key pairs, and an inadequate random number generator to generate these keys can result in little or no security. On trust anchor installation and storage: trust anchor installation and storage is critical, transmission of a trust anchor, especially self-signed certificates used as trust anchors, from the transport receiver to the transport sender for installation requires one or more out-of-band steps, care must be taken to ensure the installed trust anchor is in fact the correct trust anchor, and trust anchor information must be securely stored.
sections.plainLanguage: Four practical warnings. Do not renegotiate the connection mid-session. Accept that messages can vanish. Generate keys with a good random number source, or the encryption is worth nothing. And check the certificate you install as a trust anchor out of band, because a wrong one defeats the whole scheme.

viz.caption: THE HANDSHAKE BEFORE ANY LOG MESSAGE IS SENT

messages.label: DTLS CLIENT HELLO
messages.note: The transport sender initiates the connection.

messages.label: DTLS HELLO VERIFY REQUEST
messages.note: Carries a cookie, so a spoofed source address cannot cost the server resources.

messages.label: DTLS SERVER HELLO
messages.note: The handshake completes and the two sides have session keys.

messages.label: SYSLOG MESSAGE
messages.note: No syslog message may be sent before the handshake has successfully completed.

items.title: Confidentiality
items.text: Counters disclosure of the message contents.

items.title: Integrity checking
items.text: Counters modifications to a message on a hop-by-hop basis.

items.title: Authentication
items.text: Server or mutual authentication counters masquerade.

items.title: Cookie exchange
items.text: Counters denial of service attacks during the handshake.

viz.caption: ABNF OF THE DTLS APPLICATION DATA FOR SYSLOG

data.title: Application data grammar
data.code:
APPLICATION-DATA = 1*SYSLOG-FRAME

SYSLOG-FRAME = MSG-LEN SP SYSLOG-MSG

MSG-LEN = NONZERO-DIGIT *DIGIT

SP = %d32

NONZERO-DIGIT = %d49-57

DIGIT = %d48 / NONZERO-DIGIT

items.title: Renegotiation
items.text: It is RECOMMENDED that renegotiation be disabled for syslog over DTLS.

items.title: Message loss
items.text: The transports are unreliable, so messages can be lost or removed without the receiver knowing.

items.title: Private key generation
items.text: An inadequate random number generator can result in little or no security.

items.title: Trust anchor installation
items.text: Care must be taken to ensure the installed trust anchor is in fact the correct trust anchor.
